correctness.rationale: Theorem verified analytically: \(R^{\mathsf T}R=A+2I\) and \(RR^{\mathsf T}=(n-2)I+\mathbf1\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}\) give three orthogonal eigenprojections; positivity of sinks makes their non-dark complement exponentially decaying. The constant projector has restricted rank one. The centered unsigned-incidence restricted rank is \(n-b(F)-\varepsilon(F)\), via componentwise alternating-kernel vectors and the balanced-bipartition criterion. The -2 eigenprojector restricted rank is \(|F|-b(\overline F)\), using injectivity of R^T. Their sum is the boxed formula for all \(n\ge5\) and every nonempty F. The C4/paw comparison follows from complementary nonbipartite connectivity and the graph-component counts. The actual standalone script passed 2531 independent finite comparisons; finite tests do not prove the infinite theorem.

originality.rationale: The proposition is a closed, graph-combinatorial evaluation of the full arbitrary-multi-sink bright rank in the triangular quantum-walk family, not the already established abstract spectral-overlap method. Accessible primary full text concerns single-trap transport or Hermitian quantum search; the result also differs in objects from previously studied Hamming two-monitor and joined-cycle models. Multiple focused published-finding corpus searches showed adjacent Johnson-scheme concentration and incidence sampling topics, not the stated complementary-bipartite-component absorption classification. General linear-algebraic observability and incomplete documents remain candid residual risks.

value.rationale: Absorption from a maximally mixed single-excitation state is a physically motivated transport measure and equals the exact dimension of the accessible spectral subspace divided by network size. Arbitrary trap sets are classified structurally in a single expression using both trap and complement bipartiteness, and balanced components yield a nonobvious extra correction. The four-trap quadrilateral vs paw difference demonstrates a concrete topology-sensitive loss of a bright mode, a natural design question; complete classification has value beyond coding, correctness or a tiny numerical difference.
